scenes.tts: A nucleotide is one of the most expensive small molecules a cell makes. Nucleotides are the letters of DNA and RNA, and the carriers of energy, ATP and GTP. They form the cores of signaling molecules like cyclic A M P. They also form the backbones of cofactors such as N A D plus, F A D, and coenzyme A. Building their rings from scratch costs a small fortune in ATP. So the cell almost never throws one away.
scenes.narration: A nucleotide is one of the most expensive small molecules a cell makes. Nucleotides are the letters of DNA and RNA, and the carriers of energy, ATP and GTP. They form the cores of signaling molecules like cyclic AMP. They also form the backbones of cofactors such as NAD⁺, FAD, and coenzyme A. Building their rings from scratch costs a small fortune in ATP. So the cell almost never throws one away.

scenes.tts: There are two routes to a purine nucleotide, and the difference is mostly about cost. De novo synthesis builds the purine ring atom by atom, directly onto an activated ribose called P R P P. It runs about ten enzymatic steps and spends roughly six ATP to make the first finished purine nucleotide, I M P. Both A M P and G M P branch from I M P.
scenes.narration: There are two routes to a purine nucleotide, and the difference is mostly about cost. De novo synthesis builds the purine ring atom by atom, directly onto an activated ribose called PRPP. It runs about ten enzymatic steps and spends roughly six ATP to make the first finished purine nucleotide, IMP. Both AMP and GMP branch from IMP.

scenes.tts: Salvage takes a free base that already exists, such as hypoxanthine, guanine, or adenine, and reattaches it to P R P P in a single step. The enzyme H G P R T salvages hypoxanthine and guanine. A P R T salvages adenine. Recycling is so much cheaper that cells recover something like ninety percent of their free purines. Salvage is the default.
scenes.narration: Salvage takes a free base that already exists, such as hypoxanthine, guanine, or adenine, and reattaches it to PRPP in a single step. The enzyme HGPRT salvages hypoxanthine and guanine. APRT salvages adenine. Recycling is so much cheaper that cells recover something like ninety percent of their free purines. Salvage is the default.

scenes.tts: Now imagine the recycling is gone. In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked defect, H G P R T is missing. Free bases that should have been reclaimed are dumped into the catabolic pathway and turned into uric acid. The P R P P that salvage would have used piles up and pushes de novo synthesis even higher. That makes still more purines to degrade. The result is severe hyperuricemia alongside profound neurological disease.
scenes.narration: Now imagine the recycling is gone. In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked defect, HGPRT is missing. Free bases that should have been reclaimed are dumped into the catabolic pathway and turned into uric acid. The PRPP that salvage would have used piles up and pushes de novo synthesis even higher. That makes still more purines to degrade. The result is severe hyperuricemia alongside profound neurological disease.

scenes.tts: When a purine is finally retired, it is taken apart down a short tail. A M P and adenosine funnel through inosine to hypoxanthine. Then the enzyme xanthine oxidase oxidizes hypoxanthine to xanthine, and xanthine to uric acid. Guanine joins the route one step later, at xanthine. Most mammals carry uricase, which converts uric acid into highly soluble allantoin. Humans and the other great apes lost a working uricase during evolution. For us, uric acid is the end product, and it is only sparingly soluble.

Most mammals carry uricase, which converts uric acid into highly soluble allantoin. Humans and the other great apes lost a working uricase during evolution. For us, uric acid is the end product, and it is only sparingly soluble.

scenes.tts: That single missing enzyme is why we get gout. Once serum urate climbs past roughly 6.8 milligrams per deciliter, it begins to crystallize as monosodium urate. Those needle-sharp crystals in a joint are the flare. The fix is to make less of it. Allopurinol, a hypoxanthine look-alike, inhibits xanthine oxidase, so urate production falls and the crystals can dissolve. Gertrude Elion and George Hitchings designed it by reasoning about the enzyme.
